title: A Front Divided
subtitle: The campaign’s situation at the close of Phase II
author: R.G. Cruise
phase: II — The Drive into the Soviet Interior
summary: The German turn south developed alongside Soviet offensives, withdrawals and defensive preparations elsewhere. Replacement movements, vehicle repair, maritime supply and civilian labour determined how far the next orders could be carried out.
body:
At 02:35 on 25 August 1941, Stalin and Shaposhnikov issued a directive requiring the Soviet Western Front to continue its offensive and defeat the German grouping around Smolensk. The document assigned objectives to six armies, set a timetable extending into September and required cooperation with the Reserve Front. At the same time, German forces were beginning the larger movement southward authorised four days earlier. Neither command could treat its chosen offensive as the only operation that mattered across the central theatre. The German redirection did not leave the central front empty, and the Soviet decision to attack did not mean that the forces receiving the order possessed everything necessary to carry it out. [1] [2] The atlas’s second phase closes at a point of increasing operational divergence. The northern armies were fighting around Lake Ilmen, Leningrad’s approaches and Tallinn. In the centre, German formations met renewed Soviet attacks while striking power moved south. In Ukraine, the defeat at Uman had opened further routes without ending resistance at Kiev or Odessa. The concluding question is how these concurrent tasks affected usable strength. The answer connects replacements and repair to command, transport and civilian labour, showing why the territory held on 25 August provides only part of the balance between the armies and the societies sustaining them.

Smolensk remained a battlefield

Stavka interpreted the German concentration against the Bryansk Front as apparently directed towards Bryansk and Zhizdra, while German forces held the Bely, Vyazma and Spas-Demensk directions. That assessment identifies both recognition of a danger and uncertainty about its intended development. The high command had to issue instructions before the subsequent southward drive supplied the clarity available to later historians. Reading the directive in those circumstances helps explain the allocation of Soviet effort: commanders were responding to several plausible threats while attempting to exploit German commitments elsewhere. The source’s own qualification must remain part of the reconstructed decision. [1] The Western Front’s response was to keep pressure on the German position around Smolensk. The 29th Army was directed toward Velizh. The 30th was to support the 19th Army’s attack on Dukhovshchina, north of Smolensk. The 19th Army was then to turn southwest toward the city’s area while avoiding a frontal assault on Smolensk itself. This sequence sought to undo the German position through connected movements, rather than simply send all available troops toward the same urban objective. The northern approach, the city’s communications and the neighbouring armies’ progress had to be understood together. [1] South and east of those formations, the 16th Army was to attack toward Kardymovo and Smolensk in support of the 19th and 20th Armies. The 20th Army’s initial direction ran through the Klimova and Ryabtsevo station areas before turning northwest. These orders attempted to create converging pressure against the Smolensk–Yartsevo grouping. A railway station in such a directive was more than a convenient place name: it marked a communications point around which movement, supply and defensive positions might be organised. Reaching it required fighting through the German forces protecting the same network. [1] The 22nd Army had a different and urgent responsibility. It was ordered to deal with German mobile forces that had penetrated its area and to secure the offensive’s northern flank around the Velikiye Luki sector. Air and tank support were specified for this task. The wider attack therefore depended partly on restoring a situation already deteriorating at one end of the front. A headquarters could order offensive action in the centre while requiring defensive recovery on its flank, but both tasks competed for the limited formations and supporting arms available. [1] The execution provisions sought to prevent the disconnections that had impaired earlier attacks. Continuous reconnaissance of open flanks would improve warning; immediate fortification of captured positions would help retain gains; coordinated infantry, artillery, tank and air action would connect fire support to movement. These were interdependent requirements. A formation that advanced without securing its new position might lose the ground before the next stage began, while support arriving at the wrong time could leave infantry exposed. The directive records an effort to apply experience, with actual improvement depending on whether formations possessed the staff work, training and equipment needed to realise it. [1]

What the centre could still sustain

The planned offensive also required cooperation with Zhukov’s Reserve Front. Its left wing was to attack from 30 August, with the 24th Army directed against the Yelnya grouping and toward Pochinok, and the 43rd Army toward Roslavl. Those were future tasks as seen on 25 August. The broader Smolensk campaign therefore extended beyond this chapter’s endpoint, and the later fighting around Yelnya cannot be treated as already completed. The directive simultaneously required the Reserve Front to continue developing a deeper defensive belt. Preparation for attack and preparation for another German advance existed within the same order. [1] The German centre consequently retained important obligations while its principal mobile effort shifted south. Infantry had to hold the existing line, artillery had to support that defence, and reserves had to respond to Soviet penetrations. The forces protecting the southern movement’s flank were also unavailable for other tasks. The image of a complete pause before Moscow obscures this expenditure. Even where an army group gained little territory, fighting could continue to consume ammunition, experienced infantry, vehicles and the time needed to rebuild units for a later offensive. [2] German personnel accounting provides a useful distinction between replacements assigned and replacements received. The Army’s retrospective study records 146,000 replacements reaching the eastern theatre between 22 June and 25 August: 66,000 for Army Group Centre, 52,000 for South and 28,000 for North. The same table separately lists further arrivals during 25–31 August and men still expected afterward. Those later categories cannot be added to the strength available on the twenty-fifth. The table illustrates a recurring problem throughout this phase: resources existed at several points in a system, but only some had reached the formations that needed them. [3] The replacement table measures arrivals in the theatre, leaving the further process of integration to be established. Men had to reach units, acquire assignments and enter formations that could also lack officers, specialists or transport. Their presence could replenish numbers without immediately restoring previous cohesion. Repair involved a comparable sequence, with the 18 August memorandum already warning that emergency rehabilitation would permit only limited further movement. German strength therefore depended on work whose stages occupied different places and times. This distinction explains how substantial resources could be moving towards the armies while commanders still faced restricted possibilities for the next operation. [3] Soviet regeneration likewise depended on more than the creation of new designations. Formations required experienced staffs, artillery and dependable communications if their combined resources were to influence the battle effectively. The detailed coordination provisions in the Western Front’s orders addressed those requirements, while repeated losses made them harder to satisfy. The capacity to assemble further armies prolonged resistance; their uneven readiness helped determine its cost. This relationship between institutional resilience and operational weakness runs through the phase and explains why Germany repeatedly encountered substantial opposition after victories that appeared to have exhausted it. [2] [1]

Retreat and recovery south of Lake Ilmen

The northern front supplied a particularly clear record of what such adaptation looked like under pressure. The counteroffensive around Staraya Russa had forced a German response, but by 23–25 August the Soviet 11th Army was withdrawing behind the Lovat. Its war diary describes a relatively organised movement by its own formations alongside serious disorder in the neighbouring 34th Army. These descriptions come from one army’s headquarters and need to retain that perspective. They nevertheless show why the outcome cannot be reduced to a single arrow moving eastward across the map. [4] The 180th and 254th Rifle Divisions were assigned sectors on the eastern bank of the Lovat, while the 182nd and 183rd Divisions were to assemble farther back in army reserve. Elements remained temporarily at crossings and bridgeheads until relieving units arrived. The 21st Motorised Rifle Regiment also crossed to the eastern bank and covered a broad sector by blocking the most important approaches. This was a defence organised around usable routes rather than a uniformly occupied line. The river provided an obstacle, but the army still had to control crossing places and maintain contact between its reduced formations. [4] Movement was restricted by air attack and the need to conceal troops. The diary records an instruction preventing units from continuing their marches in daylight on 24 August; they were to remain where dawn found them and resume after darkness. This restriction changed the pace of withdrawal and regrouping. A division ordered to assemble farther east could be physically moving toward its destination while remaining unavailable there for much of the day. The resulting delay was not explained by distance alone. Air superiority affected the hours during which roads could be used and therefore the rate at which a new defence could be established. [4] The lack of reliable information about 34th Army on the left complicated 11th Army’s regrouping. A liaison report received by 25 August described separated soldiers filling roads and woods and a neighbouring headquarters unable to locate its previous day’s front precisely. Staff officers were collecting men and directing them behind the Lovat. These activities show recovery beginning within disintegration: personnel still existed, but returning them to usable military strength required reunion with units, orders and supplies. The neighbouring army’s uncertain position also affected the protection available to 11th Army, making the restoration of command a problem extending beyond either headquarters alone. [4]

Morozov’s missing division

Vasily Morozov’s 11th Army could not assign the 202nd Motorised Division a definite task during part of its regrouping because headquarters lacked information about its whereabouts. By the end of 24 August, the diary located it near Malye Dubovitsy. Morozov then sent its commander a personal note requiring concentration near Bolshiye Dubovitsy by the following morning.

The episode is small enough to disappear in an army-level summary, yet it captures a basic condition of command. A formation listed in an order of battle was not necessarily a formation whose location was known or whose movement could be controlled. The note represents a documented effort to restore that connection. It does not establish that every element of the division reached the destination on time. The distinction helps explain why headquarters repeatedly used messengers and personal intervention alongside formal orders. [4]

The approaches to Leningrad and Tallinn

Farther north, Army Group North’s movement toward Leningrad remained divided among routes approaching from the west, the Luga area and the Lake Ilmen sector. Soviet resistance and the counterattacks farther south complicated the concentration of German forces. The difficulty was not simply taking the next town. An advancing force had to keep its connections open while neighbouring formations dealt with different terrain and different enemy groupings. The fighting near Staraya Russa mattered to Leningrad because it competed for German strength that might otherwise have supported the advance toward the city. [3] Tallinn presented a separate coastal problem. German forces had reached the Gulf of Finland near Kunda on 7 August, cutting the land connection from Tallinn toward Leningrad. The remaining Soviet position depended on maritime communications. Within that position were military formations, naval personnel, industrial workers and civilians with sharply different relationships to Soviet power. The Estonian Maritime Museum’s account emphasises that thousands of Estonian men had been compulsorily mobilised. A ship leaving the port could therefore carry people escaping German attack alongside people being removed from their country against their will. [5] The approach to Tallinn also required infantry fighting that an image of uninterrupted German mechanised advance would miss. Toomas Hiio’s study of the Kiviloo battle identifies the 3rd Battalion of the German 162nd Infantry Regiment, 61st Infantry Division, fighting on 22 August against elements of the 1st Estonian Rifle Regiment formed from Soviet destruction battalions. Those forces were covering a withdrawal toward Tallinn. Hiio also shows how the sparse road and railway network constrained the movement of German infantry, ammunition and supplies, while air support competed with priorities toward Leningrad. Local action and transport capacity helped determine the pace of the larger advance. [6] Tallinn’s major evacuation remained ahead on 25 August. The convoys departed on the twenty-eighth, and the maritime disaster near Juminda unfolded on 28–29 August. The prior loss of land communications had already made the port dependent on a sea exit, but the future losses cannot be treated as knowledge shared by those preparing to leave. Commanders had to preserve an embarkation area while organising shipping. For civilians and forcibly mobilised men, access to that shipping could combine escape from German attack with removal under Soviet authority. The meaning of departure depended on the person’s circumstances as well as on the operation’s military purpose. [5]

The work of preparing a city

Lena Mukhina before the blockade

In her diary, Lena Mukhina recorded three hours unloading a barge of bricks on 5 July as compulsory labour. On 9 August she noted four hours digging trenches along the Obvodny Canal. The Russian extracts published by Ogonyok preserve dated observations made before the September land blockade. They place an adolescent’s time and physical effort within Leningrad’s defensive preparations, alongside her wish to help her mother. The entries establish these particular activities, without measuring the total labour she performed or the experience of every young resident. Their value is the connection between a city’s defence and the individual work through which part of it was built.

[7]

Ukraine after Uman

In the south, the destruction of the Soviet grouping around Uman had removed a major obstacle to the German advance, but it had not completed Army Group South’s objectives. Soviet forces withdrawing eastward sought to preserve crossings over the Dnieper and establish another line. German plans called for bridgeheads at places including Cherkassy, Kremenchug and Dnepropetrovsk. Each crossing offered access to further operations while creating a new position that had to be supplied and defended. A bridgehead was the beginning of another logistical problem as well as an operational opportunity. [3] Kiev remained connected to a different danger. The German 6th Army faced resistance around the city and from the Soviet 5th Army farther north, while the advance of the 2nd Army and 2nd Panzer Group from the Gomel direction threatened the wider rear. The strategic choice examined in The Decision to Turn South was now becoming a movement that Soviet commands had to counter. The Soviet Central Front was being dissolved and its surviving forces incorporated into the Bryansk Front, adding another organisational transition to an already unstable operational situation. [2] These headquarters changes could clarify responsibility, but they also had to be implemented among armies with damaged communications and uncertain positions. A surviving unit needed to know where to report, which route to use and which neighbouring formation could protect its flank. The problems documented around Gomel did not end when the army’s superior headquarters changed. Orders to defend Kiev and the Dnieper continued to coexist with the effort to contain a threat developing farther north and east. On 25 August, the future September pocket was a danger being created through movement, not a completed enclosure. [2] Odessa remained a defended coastal position outside the main Soviet line. The Romanian 4th Army’s approach had developed into a sustained struggle, while the Soviet garrison retained a connection to the Black Sea Fleet. Stavka’s directive of 19 August placed Rear Admiral Gavriil Zhukov in command of the Odessa Defence Region under the fleet commander. The arrangement recognised the dependence of land defence on ships, coastal facilities and maritime supply. It offered an organisational answer to the problem of coordinating services whose immediate responsibilities had previously been divided. [8] [9] Odessa’s continued defence depended on making the sea connection function through its successive stages. Cargo had to be assembled, shipped, discharged and carried from the port to the positions requiring it; outward movement had to accommodate wounded soldiers and civilians as well as other demands. This organisation gave the coastal force possibilities unavailable to the armies trapped at Uman, but each stage remained vulnerable to interruption. The contrast turns attention from the shape of a defended area to the capacity of its remaining connections. Holding a port had military value through the traffic it could sustain under attack. [9]

Civilians within the operational system

The Leningrad diary and the Estonian accounts bring individual experience into systems that military documents commonly describe as resources. Defensive preparation required labour, food, shelter and movement, while the people providing them acted under different combinations of conviction, obligation and coercion. Mukhina’s compulsory work and the removal of mobilised Estonian men should not be collapsed into one form of participation. Each belongs to a particular institutional setting and personal situation. Together they show why an account of military capacity needs evidence about how that capacity was obtained and what its demands meant for those outside the fighting formations. Occupation brought further divisions that a map of military control could not represent. The earlier studies of Uman and Gomel have followed prisoners, evacuation and the beginning of anti-Jewish persecution in specific places. Their significance at the end of August was cumulative. German territorial gains placed additional communities within reach of institutions pursuing exploitation and racial violence; Soviet retreat simultaneously disrupted the arrangements on which escape depended. The Uman study and Gomel study retain the detailed evidence and chronology of those local consequences. They are part of the operational balance because the capture of territory changed who could leave, who could be compelled to work and who was exposed to murder. Soviet coercion also crossed the boundary between the front and the household. Order No. 270, issued on 16 August, threatened families with punishment connected to soldiers’ surrender or officers’ classification as deserters. As armies withdrew and units lost contact, the official treatment of capture could compound the uncertainty faced by relatives. The policy should not be used to explain every soldier’s conduct, but it establishes that military failure could bring penalties imposed by the soldier’s own state as well as captivity under the enemy. Responsibility belongs to the institutions and decisions documented in each case. [10] The movement of people and the movement of armies consequently cannot be separated into independent narratives. A railway might be needed for replacements, evacuated machinery and families seeking safety. A road usable by a retreating regiment might also carry civilians and wounded men. A headquarters could order a withdrawal without being able to provide every person along its route with transport. These pressures help explain why a successful evacuation, an orderly military movement and the survival of a particular household did not necessarily coincide. The relevant measure was access to a functioning route at the necessary time, under conditions that were changing from day to day.

The war’s external connections

The effort to sustain the Soviet Union was beginning to take a more tangible maritime form. Convoy Dervish had departed Liverpool on 12 August and continued from Iceland on the twenty-first, bound for Archangel. On 25 August it was still in transit; it would arrive on 31 August. That sequence prevents the convoy’s cargo from being counted as supplies already available to the armies described here. It also shows how the campaign was becoming connected to a longer transport system involving merchant shipping, naval escorts, ports and onward distribution. Political agreement was only the beginning of that chain. [11] On the chapter’s anchor date, Britain and the Soviet Union also invaded Iran. Reza Shah appealed to Roosevelt on 25 August, presenting the attack as aggression against a neutral country and rejecting the invading governments’ justification concerning Germans resident in Iran. His appeal invoked international justice and the rights of peoples. The document records Iran’s ruler making a diplomatic case for intervention; it is not an independent account of every military incident he described. It nevertheless places Iranian sovereignty and civilian exposure to attack within a story often told only as the development of Allied cooperation. [12] The American minister in Tehran, Louis Dreyfus, reported that the Shah had offered further assurances about expelling Germans and asked what Britain and the Soviet Union would provide in return for his concessions. Dreyfus also stated that reliable news of the fighting was still lacking, while describing comparatively normal activity in Tehran and British aircraft dropping leaflets. The report preserves the uneven information available during the opening day. Diplomatic discussions, military intervention and daily urban life were proceeding simultaneously, and observers in the capital could not yet offer a complete account of the invasion’s effects. [13] Concern extended beyond Iran. In Washington, the Turkish ambassador Mehmet Münir Ertegün told Wallace Murray that he feared the consequences of expanding Soviet power and doubted British assurances. He expressly spoke without instructions from his government, so his remarks cannot be presented as an official Turkish policy decision. They show the anxiety that cooperation against Germany could generate in neighbouring states. The alliance’s strategic purposes did not dissolve other countries’ concerns about sovereignty, territorial security or the possibility that their interests would be sacrificed to the larger war. [14]

The position on 25 August

By the end of the phase, German forces retained the initiative in important sectors and the capacity to inflict further severe defeats. Their strength was also distributed among defence against Soviet attacks, rehabilitation, protection of communications and a new manoeuvre into Ukraine. Soviet losses had repeatedly disrupted armies, yet regrouping, new formations and the recovery of separated personnel continued to produce resistance. This interaction explains the unfinished campaign more precisely than territorial totals alone. German success remained substantial, while its conversion into a final decision required further operations against an opponent still able to reconstruct part of the military power already destroyed. The next stage would test the German attempt to cut the communications behind Kiev, the Soviet effort to renew pressure around Smolensk and the capacity of the northern defences to preserve Leningrad’s approaches. Tallinn’s evacuation and Dervish’s arrival were still future events on 25 August; September’s encirclements and counteroffensives also remained to be fought. The next orders would have to be carried out by formations whose condition varied sharply: some were assembling, others withdrawing, repairing vehicles or remaining engaged along fronts the larger strategic manoeuvre had not made quiet. Civilians confronted the same changing connections with far less power to secure them, making the continuation of military operations inseparable from the conditions of survival.

sourceMethod: Numbered citations lead to the sources below; each entry lists the passages cited and links back to its first use. Numbered references link to the bibliography and return to their first use. Specific document, paragraph and page locators accompany the references. Soviet military records were read in Russian transcription from the published General Staff collections; English descriptions are paraphrases by the atlas, and archival identifiers are those printed in the collections, not claims of direct archival inspection. Orders establish intentions; situation reports contain contemporary information, estimates and gaps. U.S. Army retrospective studies are read critically alongside Soviet records and other scholarship. Publisher excerpts are cited only for inspected passages. Testimony is distinguished from contemporary reporting. Dates in titles anchor the chronology; subsequent developments are dated explicitly. The atlas layers are qualified regional interpretations; their boundaries and arrows are not independent evidence of exact control or unit positions.
